episodes.text: Father, Aung San, was assassinated by political rivals when she was two years old; she was raised largely on his posthumous reputation, and her mother separately became a prominent public figure (ambassador to India and Nepal), giving her a second high-profile parental influence.

Completed an Oxford undergraduate degree with only third-class honours -- a specifically unexceptional result -- then spent 1968-71 in an administrative, non-political UN budget role and, in 1985-87, pursued purely literary graduate research (Burmese literature at SOAS) with no indication at the time of preparing for a political career.

In her own essay "Freedom from Fear," explicitly held up her father's willingness "to speak the truth, to stand by his word, to accept criticism, to admit his faults, to correct his mistakes, to respect the opposition, to parley with the enemy and to let people be the judge of his worthiness as a leader" as the model for confronting fear.

Returned to Burma in March 1988 solely to nurse her mother after a stroke, with no stated political intention; within six months she had addressed a half-million-person rally at the Shwedagon Pagoda calling for democratic government, explicitly framing her own entry into politics as "I could not as my father's daughter remain indifferent to all that was going on."

Co-founded the National League for Democracy (Sept 1988) built substantially from retired senior military officers (Aung Gyi as president, Tin Oo as vice-president) rather than solely civilian dissidents, taking the general-secretary post herself; within three months (Dec 1988) Aung Gyi resigned, publicly alleging communist infiltration -- an early, documented internal leadership rupture.
Undertook a nationwide speech-making tour to large audiences in late 1988 in direct defiance of a government ban on political gatherings.

Later explicitly clarified, in a 2007 statement, that her commitment to nonviolent methods rested on "political and practical reasons rather than moral grounds" -- framing a strategy widely read as an ethical commitment as, in her own words, a calculated tactical choice.

In April 1989 at Danubyu, facing soldiers under a captain's written orders to open fire, motioned her own followers off to the side of the road while she herself continued walking directly toward the levelled rifles; the order to fire was countermanded only as she approached, and she walked through the line of soldiers.

After soldiers seized roughly 40 NLD members following her first house arrest (July 1989), undertook a twelve-day hunger strike specifically demanding humane treatment for the detained members (and reportedly asked to be imprisoned alongside them), losing about twelve pounds and requiring intravenous nourishment before ending the strike once the junta promised fair treatment.
Was repeatedly offered release from house arrest on condition of leaving the country and repeatedly refused, a pattern that recurred across multiple separate detention periods from 1989 through 2010.

The National League for Democracy won a landslide 1990 election victory (roughly 80-82% of parliamentary seats) while she remained under house arrest and unable to campaign in person; the junta refused to recognize or transfer power despite the result.

Some party colleagues (including ex-military figures) who had joined the NLD during the 1988 crisis left the party during this period, reportedly believing her more confrontational stance toward the military conflicted with a genuinely nonviolent approach -- her own tactical positioning cost her some allied support rather than uniting her coalition.

Was awarded the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize while under house arrest and unable to travel to accept it (her sons accepted on her behalf); directed the full US$1.3 million prize money into a health and education trust for the Burmese people rather than retaining it personally.
While nominally free between detentions in the mid-1990s, maintained a sustained, regular practice of addressing supporters gathered at her house gate every weekend.

In November 1996 her motorcade was attacked by roughly 200 men wielding chains, batons, and stones, reportedly paid a small sum each by a pro-junta organization; a police complaint was filed but no action was taken against the attackers.

Despite sustained international appeals (including from the UN Secretary-General, the Pope, and the US government) to allow her dying husband Michael Aris a final visit, the government instead offered that she herself leave Burma to see him; she declined, reasoning she would not be allowed to re-enter, and he died in Oxford in March 1999 without seeing her again since 1995.

Publicly framed the cost of choosing political commitment over family in explicitly comparative terms: "As a mother, the greater sacrifice was giving up my sons, but I was always aware of the fact that others had given up more than me" -- describing her own significant personal loss by measuring it against others' losses rather than presenting it as uniquely severe.

Was separated from her two sons (who remained in the United Kingdom) for an extended period as a direct consequence of her decision to remain politically engaged in Burma, not reunited with them in-country until 2011.
Was released in May 2002 after roughly 19 months of house arrest following UN-facilitated confidence-building negotiations, and publicly declared "a new dawn for the country" on release.

In May 2003 her motorcade was ambushed near Depayin by a mob organized by pro-junta militias who blocked the road; at least 70 people in her convoy were killed, and a later (2015) account by the former junta's own Secretary-1 stated the ruling council's chairman had directly ordered the convoy stopped "by all means." She and her driver escaped the immediate ambush but were arrested shortly afterward.

Was held in secret detention at Insein Prison for over three months after the Depayin ambush, underwent a hysterectomy during this period, and was then moved to house arrest rather than continued prison detention; a subsequent 2008 house-arrest extension was characterized by international legal observers as itself illegal under both international and Burmese domestic law.

During the 2007 Saffron Revolution, made a brief unscheduled public appearance at her residence gate -- still under house arrest -- to receive blessings from a column of Buddhist monks marching for human rights, despite the restriction on her movement and contact.

After an uninvited American swam to her residence in May 2009 and stayed two nights against her control, she was tried for violating house-arrest terms in a proceeding documented as procedurally one-sided (defense allowed only one of four proposed witnesses against fourteen prosecution witnesses; proposed character witnesses rejected); convicted and sentenced to three years hard labor, immediately commuted to 18 months further house arrest -- a sentence whose timing prevented her participation in the 2010 election.

Spent her 64th birthday (2009) in detention during this same trial, sharing biryani rice and a chocolate cake with her prison guards -- a small documented human detail of her conduct within an adversarial custodial relationship.

Across roughly 15 of 21 years (1989-2010) under house arrest, maintained a consistent daily routine of pre-dawn meditation, extensive reading (Buddhism, philosophy, biographies of Gandhi/Nehru/Mandela specifically), and household chores while following outside news via BBC radio broadcasts, without telephone, computer, or internet access for most of the period.

Practiced piano regularly (reportedly Mozart) in the earlier part of her detention, but stopped once Burma's humidity warped the instrument and put it permanently out of tune -- an activity abandoned due to environmental constraint rather than choice.

Once genuine political-reform signals appeared after her 2010 release, pivoted directly and quickly to diplomatic engagement with reforming government figures and foreign leaders (a 2011 phone conference with US President Obama, a December 2011 in-person meeting with Secretary of State Clinton) despite decades spent opposing that same governing system.

Immediately upon the NLD's decisive November 2015 election win, is documented as having personally "laid down the law" on party discipline to newly elected NLD members of parliament -- asserting strict top-down control at the very moment of the party's greatest electoral mandate rather than a looser, more collegial transition.

As State Counsellor, ordinary NLD parliamentarians were required to clear even routine floor questions with party leadership before raising them, a specific granular bottleneck; colleagues separately described her management approach as running her party "like a dictator" who "doesn't listen, or accept advice," and a former US ambassador identified a consistent pattern of top-down leadership and decision-making gridlock.

Two of her cabinet ministers (Finance and Commerce) held credentials from unaccredited diploma-mill-type institutions; despite public ridicule over the appointments, she did not replace either minister.

Made no known arrangements for a political successor despite being in her early seventies and personally dominating party decision-making at every level; the NLD under her leadership enforced strict internal party discipline in which questioning government positions was actively discouraged and a member who publicly criticized the military's political role received no defense from party leadership.

In ethnic-minority regions, ran NLD candidates without consulting local ethnic party leaders and used constitutional provisions to install NLD-appointed chief ministers even where local ethnic parties had won the popular vote; separately insisted on naming a Mon State bridge after her already widely-memorialized father despite local public demonstrations against the choice, after which the NLD's support in the area fell by roughly half in the next by-election, losing the seat.

Publicly declared ethnic peace the 'national priority' and explicitly linked its progress to constitutional amendments, even though the military held a constitutionally guaranteed veto-capable parliamentary bloc -- a foreseeably self-defeating sequencing choice; subsequent peace conferences under her leadership produced no new agreement signatories while conflict intensified in Rakhine and Shan States.

In October 2016 personally requested the lifting of most remaining US economic sanctions on Myanmar, removing a major piece of external leverage over the military leadership before the Rohingya crisis reached its most severe phase; separately, her government held a sufficient parliamentary majority to reform a criminal-defamation law used to imprison dozens of critics, but did not do so.

Her government did not issue a coherent economic policy statement until roughly four months after taking office, and did not prioritize rural electrification (despite two-thirds of the country lacking access) until over a year into her term; foreign direct investment fell substantially during her government's first year.

From August 2017 onward, following military operations against Rohingya communities that international investigators characterized as involving mass killing, rape, and arson, maintained public silence on the specific military conduct for an extended period, avoided interviews with domestic Myanmar journalists throughout her tenure, and refused to publicly acknowledge that the armed forces had committed the atrocities alleged.

An official government Facebook page under her administration dismissed a Rohingya woman's sexual-assault allegation against security forces as a 'fake rape' story; her government separately prosecuted journalists covering the crisis and restricted independent press access to the conflict zone.

During the 2015 election campaign, before the crisis reached its most severe documented phase, largely avoided discussing the Rohingya issue at all, a choice observers attributed to awareness that a more sympathetic stance would cost electoral support among the Buddhist-majority electorate.

In December 2019 personally led Myanmar's legal delegation to the International Court of Justice and delivered a roughly 30-minute speech defending Myanmar against Rohingya genocide allegations herself, rather than delegating the case entirely to lawyers or subordinate officials.

At the ICJ, directly challenged the genocide characterization, asking the court 'How can there be an ongoing genocide or genocidal intent when these concrete steps are being taken in Rakhine?' and citing development initiatives and camp closures as counter-evidence, while framing the 2017 violence as a domestic counter-insurgency response to a named armed group's coordinated attacks rather than a campaign against civilians.

Argued that any individual military misconduct should be addressed through Myanmar's own domestic courts-martial rather than international adjudication, explicitly invoking the legal principle of complementarity, while distinguishing (and not entirely ruling out) the lesser possibility of disproportionate force from the much higher legal bar of genocidal intent, which she flatly denied; her delivery was documented as measured and controlled throughout.

Her ICJ appearance drew Rohingya protesters outside the court carrying a 'Stop Genocide' banner and photographs of her captioned 'Shame' and 'agent of the military' -- contemporary commentary explicitly framed the appearance as a 'remarkable recalibration' of her global reputation, from internationally idolized former political prisoner to a sitting head of government personally defending the same military that had once imprisoned her.

On 1 February 2021, was arrested by the Myanmar military in a coup rejecting her party's November 2020 election win (a result independent observers did not find fraudulent); initial charges cited walkie-talkie radios found at her residence, widely characterized by legal observers as pretextual, followed by at least five further charges over the following two months.

Was convicted across a series of separate proceedings (Dec 2021-Dec 2022) under conditions Human Rights Watch characterized as effectively predetermined from the moment of her detention, on charges including incitement, COVID-19 restriction breaches, illegal communications equipment, and corruption, accumulating a 33-year sentence later administratively reduced to 27; continued serving as NLD general secretary/chairperson from prison until the party's 2023 forced dissolution.

As of June 2026, remains in military custody more than five years after the coup, moved by the military to a 'designated residence' with no independent confirmation of her condition available to her family; the active resistance movement within Myanmar has moved substantially beyond her own nonviolent political framework in her absence, even as regional and global powers continue to treat her case as politically significant.
